title: Why Rose does not respond to Bix's sound
summary: John asks what emotional fulfillment Bix's solos give. Rose says he appreciates Bix intellectually, argues musical sounds carry conditioned symbols, and ties Bix to a romantic ideal like Guy Lombardo or Norman Rockwell.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Al, I'd like to ask you a question that interests me very much. What kind of a feeling do you get when you listen to, for instance, Big Spiderman solo? What kind of emotional fulfillment does that represent? What kind of people seem to be attracted to that kind of sound?

Well, I think that I understand the question. And, of course, as you understand, it's not my kind of people. That is, that I don't really respond emotionally to the Bix sound, although I understand it, I think. And I find it very interesting, but purely on an intellectual basis. But I don't have any visceral reaction to Bix. I feel that all of the arts, including music, is based on certain sound, on certain symbols that we are conditioned in such a way in our society so that we associate various symbols with various circumstances. I use as an illustration before we were on tape the idea of the C chord played on an organ. When you hear that chord played, even though it in itself is an abstraction, nevertheless, we all associate it almost automatically with the sound of a church. Because our conditioning has taught us to do that. And I believe that all of the sounds that we hear, or at least most of the sounds that we hear, we already have established associations with. Now, I also use the analogy of the typical romantic scene in a Hollywood color musical, in which you have a couple standing on a balcony in the moonlight, doing a song and dance, a romantic song, a stardust or something of that nature. And this is presented to us as representing the ideal in the man-woman relationship. Now, I have always felt like this is a fake ideal and that it has little or no relationship to the actual state of affairs as it exists between male and female in our society or indeed in the world. Now, I feel that the attitude that is expressed there, the ideals that are expressed there, are represented strongly in Bix's music and that he appeals largely to the same people who would respond to that kind of an image. It is also my conviction that in every society, virtually every point of view, every emotional attitude is expressed by some artist in every medium. And I further proposed that for practical purposes, such personalities as Edgar Guest and Guy Lombardo and Norman Rockwell were essentially the same, that they represented exactly the same point of view and appealed to the same people, though they worked in different idioms. Now, I know that in discussing with you that you frequently have made reference to the relationship between Bix and Gatsby as personalities.
